extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers interested in literary theory and criticism (Northrop Frye's framework)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of Northrop Frye's systematic framework for literary criticism (modes, symbolic phases, archetypal structures, and rhetorical/genre distinctions) as presented in Anatomy of Criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and method of genuine literary criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary criticism should 'derive its method from the body of literature itself' and be a systematic study distinct from personal taste or application of external ideologies (Marxist, Freudian, Jungian, neo-classical, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frye defends criticism against two anti-methods: (1) elevating 'natural taste' over scholarly learning and (2) subjecting literature to external 'pet philosophies' that deterministically read works through ready-made ideologies. Genuine criticism is akin to scientific/systematic study (like physics or history) and presumes the body of literature has a systematic nature. Frye warns critics about sweeping generalities and the emotional repugnance to schematization, stressing schematization is a tool distinct from the direct experience of literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of Modes (five modes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify literature by five 'modes'—mythic, romantic, high mimetic, low mimetic, and ironic—each identified with a literary epoch and a characteristic ethos (the protagonist's relation to humanity and environment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modes form a continuum between plot-driven and idea-driven works. Frye suggests historical progression through these modes and a possible recursion (e.g., extreme irony returning to myth). Use the protagonist's relative status and portrayal to place a work on the continuum; examples and epochal associations are given throughout the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications of the modes to Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy concerns the hero's separation from society and manifests differently across modes: mythic (death of gods), romantic (elegies mourning heroes), high mimetic (death of a noble human), low mimetic (death/sacrifice of ordinary humans evoking pathos), ironic (protagonist weak/pitiful or persecuted by society).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify tragic works by how the protagonist's status relates to humanity and environment: e.g., mythic tragedy (death of gods), high mimetic examples Othello/Oedipus, low mimetic examples Tess or Daisy Miller, ironic examples Kafka. Use these distinctions to analyze tone, stakes, and mode-appropriate motifs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications of the modes to Comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy concerns integration of society and likewise varies by mode: mythic comedy (acceptance into gods' society), romantic comedy (pastoral/idyllic integration), high mimetic comedy (protagonist constructs own society and gains honor), low mimetic comedy (social elevation often ending in marriage), ironic comedy (satire, social rejection, or savage infliction of pain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify comic works by their social resolution and setting: mythic examples (Hercules), romantic examples (pastoral idyll), high mimetic examples (Aristophanes, Shakespeare's Prospero), ironic comic examples include satire, biting social critique, or depictions of social violence (lynch mobs, murder mysteries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications of the modes to Thematic literature
rubrics_metrics.description: When intellectual content dominates over plot, thematic literature arranges by what counts as authoritative at the time: in mythical mode scripture; romantic mode chroniclers/nomadic memory; high mimetic mode national epics; low mimetic mode individualism/romantic exposition; ironic mode poet as observer emphasizing discontinuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the mode-based societal structures to analyze essays, chronicles, epics, and lyric/thematic works: e.g., The Faerie Queene and The Lusiad as high mimetic national epics; Wordsworth's Prelude as low mimetic individual-author-centered work; The Waste Land and Finnegans Wake as ironic/anti-epiphany thematic examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal/descriptive (motifs and signs) — first symbolic phase
rubrics_metrics.description: The descriptive phase (signs) points outward to external definitions and personal connotations; the literal phase (motifs) is the symbol's inward, contextual meaning within the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frye treats 'literal' nearly opposite its common use: 'literal' = contextual, horizontal (dependent on surrounding text); 'descriptive' = external/conventional meanings laid out spatially. Use the distinction to separate conventional/sign meanings from motif-based, context-specific meanings in criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal (image) — second symbolic phase
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal phase is embodied by the image and results from interplay of rhythm and harmony of signs/motifs; frequently repeated imagery sets the tonal background of a work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phase corresponds to New Criticism/formalist attention to imagery and patterning—identify dominant recurring images (e.g., the color red in Macbeth) and contrastive images that define tone. Consider rhythm/harmony relations across the text when evaluating formal meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mythical (archetype) — third symbolic phase
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the symbol as an archetype; situate it intertextually within the body of literature by tracing its heritage through prior and subsequent works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phase emphasizes convention and intertextual connections rather than unique authorial invention—criticism here traces archetypal patterns, genre conventions, and the symbol's literary kin. Frye argues that convention is vital (even verbatim repetition can be creative) and relates this approach to a 'nature' perspective in the nature vs. nurture debate about symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagogic (monad) — fourth symbolic phase
rubrics_metrics.description: The anagogic phase treats a symbol as a monad expressing the highest spiritual or transcendent meaning—the imitation of infinite social action and infinite human thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use anagogic readings to locate transcendent/universal signification in symbols (example: Dante's Beatrice as bride of Christ). Frye frames this as a lateral interconnection culminating in a perceived spiritual unity within literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'literary symbol'
rubrics_metrics.description: A literary symbol is '[a]ny unit of any literary structure that can be isolated for critical attention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a broad, text-centered definition: symbols can be words, images, motifs, structures—anything isolable for critical analysis. This definition underpins the phase-based symbolic analysis (literal/descriptive/formal/mythical/anagogic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetypal criticism: Great Chain of Being and seasonal/mythic mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize literature around analogies derived from the Great Chain of Being (divine, human, animal, vegetable, mineral, water) and the cycle of the four seasons; map seasons to genres and mythoi (Spring–Comedy–birth; Summer–Romance–youth/triumph; Autumn–Tragedy–maturity/fall; Winter–Irony–death/chaos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Great Chain imagery (divine ↔ human ↔ animal ↔ vegetable ↔ mineral ↔ water) to analyze apocalyptic (heavenly), demonic (hellish), and analogical imagery across tragic and comic visions. Place works in the cyclical mythic scheme (birth/growth/maturity/decay) to interpret their archetypal patterns, imagery sets (e.g., lamb vs. predator, Garden vs. sinister forest), and the cultural-historical positioning of genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical criticism: melos, lexis, opsis and the radical of presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetorical criticism examines melos (tonal/musical aspect), lexis (the written word between musical and visual — diction/imagery), and opsis (visual aspects). It also emphasizes the 'radical of presentation'—the idealized relation between author and audience—as the basis for four genres: epos, fiction, drama, lyric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze works by their dominant sensory emphasis (ear/melos vs eye/opsis) and by the author-audience relation: epos (author speaks directly to audience — rhythm of recurrence), fiction (author and audience hidden — continuity of meaning/prose rhythm), drama (author hidden; audience experiences directly — decorum: diction matching character/setting), lyric (speaker overheard — associative/dreamlike rhythm). Consider how melos and opsis interplay in lexis, how rhythm types map to genre, and how 'decorum' governs diction appropriate to dramatic characters.
